analysis|01-28|1986|Η καταστροφή του Τσάλεντζερ|The Challenger disaster|The mission of the Challenger itself also gave rise to discussion about science education and the public image of NASA. The participation of non-astronauts had aroused interest among students across the country. The agency's leaders wanted to show that space was accessible to many people. This interest was widespread. The participation of the teacher strengthened the link between the programme and American schools. // The space shuttle exploded 73 seconds after launch, and all seven crew members were lost, among them Christa McAuliffe. The event shocked the whole of society. President Reagan undertook to address the nation the same day. The families of the astronauts and their colleagues suffered a deep blow, and the agency organised special support. // The Rogers Commission studied the causes and found serious weaknesses in the decision-making process. Engineers had expressed concerns about how the seals behaved at low temperatures. The disaster changed the way NASA operated and is regarded today as a lesson on the safety of large technological projects. The president asked for a moment of remembrance, and the tragedy remains a teaching example. The debate over the consequences of the event continues in academic research and in public life.

analysis|01-29|1819|Ο Στάμφορντ Ράφλς φτάνει στη Σιγκαπούρη|Stamford Raffles arrives in Singapore|At the beginning of the 19th century the British East India Company was looking for trading posts in Asia, in order to secure access to the trade of the region. Stamford Raffles was an official of the company and had experience in Malaya and in Java. The area of Singapore was a small island with a particular geographical position. British ambitions in the region were great. Raffles had an interest in the natural history of Asia and in the administrative organisation of the new territories. // On 29 January 1819 Raffles landed on the island and agreed with the local authorities to found a trading post. His choice was strategic, because the island lay on an important sea route. The agreement provoked reactions from other powers in the region. The town developed quickly through trade, migration and good administrative organisation. // The trading post grew rapidly and became one of the most important ports in Asia. In 1965 Singapore left Malaysia and was proclaimed an independent state. Today the city is one of the most important economic centres of the world. Its history begins with Raffles' strategic choice. His name remains in the names of several streets and institutions in Singapore.

analysis|01-29|1886|Ο Καρλ Μπεντς παίρνει δίπλωμα για το αυτοκίνητο|Karl Benz receives a patent for the automobile|At the end of the 19th century engineers were experimenting with internal combustion engines that could power vehicles without horses. Karl Benz, an engineer in Mannheim, had worked on such a construction for years. Competition with other inventors was intense. The idea of the automobile had by then matured into practical models. The vehicle had a low speed but served as a model for the machines that followed. // On 29 January 1886 Benz secured with a patent the three-wheeled vehicle that was named the Benz Patent-Motorwagen. The vehicle had a four-stroke engine and was designed for practical use. This registration is considered the official birth of the automobile. In 1888 the inventor's wife made a long journey with the vehicle, to demonstrate its operation to the public. // The invention paved the way for the industrial production of automobiles and for the creation of large companies. The Benz company later contributed to the creation of Mercedes-Benz. Transport changed the economy, the city and everyday life profoundly. In this way 1886 remains one of the most important years in the history of technology. The development of the automobile became linked with new factories and with the growth of production in Europe.

analysis|01-29|1916|Πρώτος γερμανικός βομβαρδισμός του Παρισιού|The first German bombing of Paris|During the First World War aviation was still in its early stages, and Zeppelin airships were used for reconnaissance and attacks. Germany sought to strike the population and the cities of the Allies. Paris was an important political and military centre. The defensive forces were limited. The damage to the city was limited, but the news caused great anxiety among the population. // On 29 January 1916 German airships bombed areas of Paris, and this was the first time that the city received such an attack from the air. The damage was limited, but the event caused intense fear among the population. The inhabitants took refuge in shelters and underground spaces. The authorities strengthened the alarm systems and the shelters, and the residents were informed about the measures. // This attack showed the potential of aerial warfare and pushed countries towards developing better anti-aircraft defence. Airships were gradually replaced by aeroplanes, which were more manoeuvrable. The experience changed thinking about the protection of civilians in war. The event is regarded as a stage in the development of modern military aviation. Zeppelins proved vulnerable to anti-aircraft fire and to pursuit aircraft. The importance of the event is also seen in the way societies remember it today.

analysis|01-29|2002|Ο «άξονας του κακού»|The "axis of evil"|After the attacks of 11 September 2001, the American government shaped a strategy for the war against terrorism. This policy included actions in several countries, with growing tension in international relations. The debate over the stance towards Iraq was intense. The alliances of the United States had already begun to divide. The phrase was used by later public debate to describe the attitude of the United States. // On 29 January 2002 President George W. Bush, in his annual address to Congress, described Iraq, Iran and North Korea as the "axis of evil". The phrase provoked strong reactions, since these countries were in different situations. The speech showed the hard line of the administration. The governments of the countries reacted with statements, and tension in international relations increased. // This rhetoric was linked to the decision for military intervention in Iraq in 2003, and the discussion about the justification of that decision continues. The phrase became a symbol of the era and of the wider confrontation over international politics. Its influence on public debate was significant for years. The following year brought developments that shaped the course of international politics in the Middle East.

analysis|01-30|1862|Καθελκύεται το USS Monitor|The USS Monitor is launched|During the American Civil War both sides sought new ships that could withstand cannon fire. Shipbuilding was in a transitional period, with wood being gradually replaced by iron. John Ericsson took on the design of the new ship for the Union. Time was pressing. The design of the ship was pioneering and was studied by the navies of the time. // On 30 January 1862 the Monitor was launched at Brooklyn in New York, and it was the first American warship with a revolving turret. Its construction was relatively quick, and the ship had a low deck, which limited the target. Its turret could rotate to direct the guns. The crew of the ship was limited, with a fairly small working space. // In March 1862 the Monitor faced the CSS Virginia at the Battle of Hampton Roads, a clash regarded as the first between ironclad warships. The battle was unexpected and had no winner. This development changed the design of warships throughout the world. The Monitor remained in history as one of the most famous ships of the Civil War. It became the model for an entire type of coastal defence ship.

analysis|01-30|1933|Ο Χίτλερ γίνεται καγκελάριος|Hitler becomes chancellor|In the late 1920s Germany was in an economic crisis, with high unemployment and political instability. Adolf Hitler's National Socialist Party developed quickly and won many seats in the elections. The Weimar Republic was difficult to govern, with constant changes of government. The political forces sought alliances. The Nazi government soon abolished freedoms after the burning of the Reichstag. // On 30 January 1933 President Hindenburg appointed Hitler chancellor, in cooperation with conservative politicians who believed they could control him. This appointment gave the party control of the government. Power began to concentrate quickly. Power was gathered into the hands of the chancellor through laws that granted emergency powers. // In the following months the regime abolished freedoms, dissolved the other parties and established a dictatorship. This policy led to the Second World War and to the Holocaust. The day of the appointment is today regarded as a turning point in the European history of the twentieth century. Political opponents were prosecuted or imprisoned, and society suffered gradual political repression. This historical development is still studied by researchers and historians around the world. Sources of the period, such as documents and testimonies, are essential material for understanding the events.

analysis|01-30|1948|Δολοφονείται ο Μαχάτμα Γκάντι|Mahatma Gandhi is assassinated|After the Second World War India was on the path to independence, with intense religious tensions between Hindus and Muslims. Gandhi had led the movement of non-violent resistance and called for peace between the communities. The partition of 1947 had been accompanied by great violence. The situation remained explosive. His funeral was held on the banks of the River Yamuna, with a large crowd of people. // On 30 January 1948 Gandhi was shot in New Delhi by a nationalist, who believed that he favoured the Muslims. Gandhi died immediately, and the news caused grief throughout the country. The government declared official mourning. The murderer was tried and sentenced to death, and was executed later. // His assassination became a symbol of the need for tolerance and peace among the communities of India. His memory remains strong, and 30 January is today called Gandhi Remembrance Day. The non-violent resistance that inspired him influenced many movements around the world. The day of the murder was established as a day of remembrance and honour in India. Sources of the period, such as documents and testimonies, are essential material for understanding the events. The importance of the event is also seen in the way societies remember it today.

analysis|01-30|1972|Η «Ματωμένη Κυριακή» στο Ντέρι|"Bloody Sunday" in Derry|In the 1970s Northern Ireland was in violent conflict between Catholics and Protestants, with armed groups and police operations. The use of internment without trial had caused great discontent in the Catholic community. Many demonstrations had already been organised. Tension was constant. The march had been organised to protest peacefully against internment. // On 30 January 1972 military forces opened fire on demonstrators in Derry, in protest against internment. Thirteen people were killed, and several were wounded. The reaction in the Catholic community was intense. The soldiers' action provoked anger and many protests in Northern Ireland and in the Republic of Ireland. // The inquiry that was later carried out, the so-called Saville Inquiry, concluded that the shootings were unjustified. The event deeply affected relations between Northern Ireland and Britain. Bloody Sunday remains a symbol of the conflict known as the Troubles. The official inquiry was completed many years later, with a public apology from the British government. The importance of the event is also seen in the way societies remember it today. Understanding the context of the period helps in interpreting the decisions taken then.

analysis|01-31|1946|Το νέο Σύνταγμα της Γιουγκοσλαβίας|The new Constitution of Yugoslavia|After the Second World War Yugoslavia was led by Tito's communist partisans, who had liberated a large part of the country. The country was multinational and included different ethnic groups and religions. The organisation of the state was a basic issue. Soviet influence was significant. The federation comprised national republics with their own administration and cultural autonomy. // On 31 January 1946 the new Constitution was adopted, based on the Soviet model. The text established six federal republics, among them Serbia, Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and Macedonia. The federation had a unified administration and a central party. Tito governed the country for decades, with internal stability and a distinctive foreign policy. // This structure was maintained for decades, until national tensions led to the break-up of Yugoslavia in the 1990s. The consequences of the collapse were deep and long-lasting for the Balkans. The Constitution of 1946 is a point of reference for the history of the region. After Tito's death in 1980, national tensions gradually increased. Understanding the context of the period helps in interpreting the decisions taken then. The debate over the consequences of the event continues in academic research and in public life.

analysis|01-31|1990|Ανοίγει το πρώτο McDonald's της Μόσχας|The first McDonald's in Moscow opens|At the end of the 1980s the Soviet Union was in the period of perestroika, with reforms that opened up the economy. The appetite for private initiative and foreign investment was growing. Everyday life in Moscow was difficult, with shortages of goods. Contact with Western culture was desired. The opening of the restaurant was part of the company's international expansion into countries of the former Eastern bloc. // On 31 January 1990 the first McDonald's opened in Pushkin Square in Moscow, with thousands of citizens queuing for hours. The opening of the American restaurant symbolised the change of era. Its opening was a major event for the press and for citizens. The products were sold at prices that were affordable for most residents of the city. // The restaurant became a symbol of the new economic era and of contact with the West. The developments of the following years led to the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991. Its story is today regarded as symbolic of the cultural and economic transition of the country. Its presence is today regarded as a historic landmark of the city's transition. The debate over the consequences of the event continues in academic research and in public life.

analysis|01-31|2020|Το Ηνωμένο Βασίλειο αποχωρεί από την ΕΕ|The United Kingdom leaves the EU|In 2016 the British voted in a referendum in favour of leaving the European Union, by a margin that revealed deep divisions. The government began negotiations with Brussels on the terms of departure. The discussions on trade and customs matters were complex. The Northern Ireland border was a particularly difficult issue. The transition period allowed businesses and citizens to adjust to the new arrangements. // On 31 January 2020, at 23:00 GMT, the United Kingdom officially left the EU, marking the end of a membership that had lasted more than four decades. The transition period that followed lasted until the end of 2020. The agreement on future relations was signed in that period. The arrangements for travel and commercial transactions changed substantially compared with the past. // Brexit changed trade relations, travel and the legal position of citizens and businesses. European integration lost a major member, and discussions about the consequences continue. This moment is regarded as a turning point in Britain's relationship with Europe. The departure showed that European integration was not a one-way road for all states. This historical development is still studied by researchers and historians around the world.

analysis|02-01|1861|Το Τέξας αποσπάται από την Ένωση|Texas secedes from the Union|After the election of Lincoln, the southern states saw the freedom of slavery as a threat to their economy. Texas, with large agricultural production and many enslaved people, had serious concerns about its future. South Carolina and Mississippi had already left. The forces of secession were growing. The state convention met in an atmosphere of intense anxiety about the future of slavery. // On 1 February 1861 the state convention voted for secession, which was ratified by a referendum a few weeks later. Texas was the seventh southern state to leave. This move strengthened the new Confederacy. The Confederacy exploited Texas's participation for military and economic needs. // The secession of Texas brought the country closer to the war, which broke out in April 1861. The state became an important front for the Confederacy, with military activity along the borders. The decision left deep marks on the political and social life of the state for decades. The state returned to the Union after the war, with its readmission completed in 1870. Sources of the period, such as documents and testimonies, are essential material for understanding the events. The importance of the event is also seen in the way societies remember it today.

analysis|02-01|1865|Ο Λίνκολν υπογράφει την 13η Τροπολογία|Lincoln signs the 13th Amendment|The Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 had abolished slavery only in the states in rebellion, and it was not permanent in law. To abolish slavery across the whole country, an amendment to the Constitution was required. Lincoln pressed Congress hard to pass the text. Opposition was significant in the House of Representatives. The vote in the House required a two-thirds majority, and achieving it was arduous. // On 1 February 1865 Congress approved the 13th Amendment, and Lincoln signed it, although his signature was not required for it to take effect. The text was sent to the states for ratification. This process was important for the legal force of the abolition. The decision was incorporated into the Constitution once the states completed ratification. // The amendment was ratified at the end of 1865, and slavery was abolished permanently throughout American territory. This decision opened the way for the rights of freed citizens, although equality took much longer to achieve. The 13th Amendment is today regarded as one of the main milestones of American constitutional history. The abolition of slavery changed the legal position of millions of people in the United States. The importance of the event is also seen in the way societies remember it today.

analysis|02-01|1884|Κυκλοφορεί ο πρώτος τόμος του Λεξικού της Οξφόρδης|The first volume of the Oxford Dictionary is published|In the 19th century the English Philological Society decided to compile a complete dictionary of the English language, with historical examples of use for every word. The work was enormous and required thousands of volunteers who sent in extracts from books. James Murray took on the direction of the project. The effort lasted for decades. The work continued for decades with an ever-larger number of contributors. // On 1 February 1884 the first part of the dictionary was published, from the letter A to the word Ant. The edition aroused great interest among scholars and the public. The project was an innovation in lexicography, with historical records of the use of every word. The volunteers sent extracts from books and newspapers, so that the use of each word could be recorded. // The Oxford English Dictionary was completed in many volumes and revised several times. Today it is one of the most authoritative dictionaries of the English language, with continuous updates. The publication of the first volume is regarded as the starting point of this long undertaking. The dictionary is today regarded as one of the greatest works of English lexicography. Understanding the context of the period helps in interpreting the decisions taken then. The debate over the consequences of the event continues in academic research and in public life.

analysis|02-01|1908|Δολοφονείται ο βασιλιάς της Πορτογαλίας|The King of Portugal is assassinated|At the beginning of the 20th century Portugal faced economic problems, political instability and growing discontent. The Republicans had strong influence in the cities and demanded the abolition of the monarchy. The corruption of the political system was widely known. The royal family was being challenged. The assassination affected political life, and the government was unable to control the situation. // On 1 February 1908 King Carlos I and the heir Luís Filipe were assassinated by gunfire in Lisbon. The murder took place in a public space, and the event shocked the country. The younger son, Manuel II, succeeded to the throne. The anti-monarchists were in contact with military units and with demonstrators in the cities. // In 1910 the monarchy was abolished, and Portugal was proclaimed a republic. This development completed a political process that had begun with the assassination. Portugal remains in history as one of the countries that moved from monarchy to republic at the beginning of the century. The revolution of 1910 completed the transition and established the republic. The debate over the consequences of the event continues in academic research and in public life. This historical development is still studied by researchers and historians around the world.

analysis|02-01|1924|Η Βρετανία αναγνωρίζει τη Σοβιετική Ένωση|Britain recognises the Soviet Union|After the October Revolution of 1917, Britain had not officially recognised the new government in Moscow. Diplomatic relations were limited, with mutual suspicion. The Soviet Union wanted to secure international legitimacy and trade relations. Commercial exchange was important for the economy. Recognition opened the way to trade agreements between the two countries. // On 1 February 1924 the Labour government under MacDonald officially recognised the Soviet Union. The decision opened the way to diplomatic talks and to trade agreements. The move was of particular importance for European diplomacy. The decision was taken in a period of reduced trust and political uncertainty. // The recognition changed relations between the two countries for the following years, although trust remained limited. Tensions around communist propaganda and political influence continued to exist. This moment is regarded as a milestone in the international recognition of the Soviet Union. The relationship between the two states continued to take shape during the 1920s. This historical development is still studied by researchers and historians around the world. Sources of the period, such as documents and testimonies, are essential material for understanding the events.

analysis|02-01|1946|Ο Τρίγκβε Λι γίνεται ο πρώτος Γενικός Γραμματέας του ΟΗΕ|Trygve Lie becomes the first Secretary-General of the UN|After the founding of the United Nations, the organisation needed a leader who would coordinate the activities of the secretariat and represent the organisation internationally. The choice of its head was a matter of diplomatic balance among the great powers. The Norwegian politician Trygve Lie had served as foreign minister of his country. His leadership would be critical for the first years of the organisation's operation. His selection was a compromise, so that it would be acceptable to the great powers. // On 1 February 1946 the General Assembly, following a proposal from the Security Council, elected him the first Secretary-General. His term began with challenges, as the organisation was still testing its strength. The negotiations over his post were complex. Lie was among the first to take up duties in an international organisation with such great responsibility. // Lie played a role in the first disputes of the Cold War and in efforts for peace, such as the war in Korea. His term ended in 1952, and his resignation was the result of political pressure. The position of the first Secretary-General set the standards for the organisation's later leaders. The disagreements over his post led to changes in the functioning of international institutions.

analysis|02-01|1979|Ο Χομεϊνί επιστρέφει στην Τεχεράνη|Khomeini returns to Tehran|Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini had been in exile for about fifteen years, first in Iraq and later in France. From there he directed the opposition to the Shah, through messages and cassettes that circulated in Iran. The revolution had developed with broad popular participation. Khomeini was recognised as the central figure of the movement. His return was welcomed by a large crowd in the city, with demonstrations that lasted several days. // On 1 February 1979 Khomeini arrived in Tehran by aircraft, and the crowd greeted the leader with great enthusiasm. His return took place a few days after the Shah's departure. The new government soon began to organise itself. The opposition to the Shah had various components, such as students, trade unions and religious organisations. // A few days later battles broke out in the capital, and the military leadership withdrew from politics. In April 1979 a referendum was held that approved the Islamic Republic. This development profoundly changed Iran's position in the world and determined the country's modern political history. The new system defined the place of religion in the country's political life. The importance of the event is also seen in the way societies remember it today. Understanding the context of the period helps in interpreting the decisions taken then.

analysis|02-01|2003|Η καταστροφή του Κολούμπια|The Columbia disaster|At the beginning of 2003 the space shuttle Columbia was carrying out a scientific mission in space. During the launch on 16 January a piece of insulating material had come off the external tank and struck the wing of the craft. Engineers had expressed concerns, but the damage was not considered decisive. The mission continued its programme. The inquiry also examined the exchange of information between the agency and the engineers. // On 1 February 2003, during the return to Earth, the craft broke up over Texas, and all seven crew members were lost. The news shocked the United States and the world. The investigation that followed examined the causes of the damage. The crews of the missions were subjected to strict checks after the tragedy. // The commission that was appointed found that the damage to the wing caused the destruction during re-entry into the atmosphere, and identified problems in the agency's safety culture. The space shuttles remained grounded for about two years, with changes to procedures. The tragedy is today regarded as a lesson on safety and on listening to engineers. The mission remains in memory as an important date for safety in space. Understanding the context of the period helps in interpreting the decisions taken then.

analysis|02-02|1536|Ιδρύεται το Μπουένος Άιρες|Buenos Aires is founded|In the 16th century Spain was expanding into South America and was looking for new settlements at the mouths of great rivers. The area of the Río de la Plata was strategic for the movement of goods to Europe. Explorers had already reached the wider region. The idea of a fortified settlement was attractive. The name of the settlement was linked with the weather of the area, which was considered favourable. // On 2 February 1536 Pedro de Mendoza founded the first settlement on the banks of the river, under the name Santa María del Buen Ayre. The indigenous peoples of the region reacted strongly to the settlement, and it did not survive. The first attempt abandoned the town after a few years. The town was connected with the port and with the trade currents of Latin America. // The town was refounded later, in 1580, by Juan de Garay, and gradually developed into an important trading centre. Today Buenos Aires is the capital of Argentina and one of the largest cities in Latin America. Its history began with this first, short-lived settlement. Today the city hosts cultural institutions and large university faculties. This historical development is still studied by researchers and historians around the world.

analysis|02-02|1709|Διασώζεται ο Αλεξάντερ Σέλκιρκ|Alexander Selkirk is rescued|The Scottish sailor Alexander Selkirk served on a ship sailing in the Pacific, but he had clashed with the captain and was put ashore on an island. The island was one of the Juan Fernández Islands, off Chile. He survived alone for about four years, by hunting and fishing. The isolation was harsh, and the psychological pressure great. Selkirk recorded his activities on the island, and his accounts interested the writers of the time. // On 2 February 1709 Selkirk was rescued by a ship of the British expedition, which had come to the island for resupply. The rescue came after four years of solitude. His return to his homeland gave great publicity to his story. His stay on the island was harsh, with loneliness and great physical effort. // The story of Selkirk inspired Daniel Defoe, who wrote Robinson Crusoe in 1719. The novel became one of the best-known works of English literature. The story of Selkirk remains a symbol of survival and of loneliness on the ocean. The island of Selkirk was later renamed Robinson Crusoe Island. Sources of the period, such as documents and testimonies, are essential material for understanding the events. The importance of the event is also seen in the way societies remember it today.

analysis|02-02|1848|Η Συνθήκη της Γουαδελούπης Ιδάλγκο|The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo|After Mexico's independence, relations with the United States were strained, mainly because of the expansion of American borders to the west. In 1845 Texas was annexed by the United States, and tension escalated into conflict. The war broke out in 1846 and spread to nearly all fronts. American military superiority was clear. The treaty included arrangements for the residents of the territories that passed to the United States, with property rights. // On 2 February 1848 the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo was signed, ending the war. Mexico ceded to the United States a large part of its territory, among them California and New Mexico. The United States paid compensation, and the Rio Grande was set as the border. The United States paid an amount regarded as consideration for the lands, with considerable debate in Congress. // The treaty changed the map of North America and led to the era of the first great American expansion to the Pacific coast. The consequences for Mexico were profound, with loss of territory and population. The treaty remains an important chapter in the relations of the two countries. The treaty opened the way to a new political and economic relationship between the two countries.

analysis|02-02|1922|Εκδίδεται ο «Οδυσσέας» του Τζέιμς Τζόις|Joyce's "Ulysses" is published|At the beginning of the 1920s James Joyce lived in Paris and was completing his experimental novel. The work narrated one day in Dublin, with interior monologues and a strongly experimental use of language. The literary community was divided over its form. His earlier books had already been discussed. The work was a constant source of inspiration for writers and critics of the time. // On 2 February 1922, the author's birthday, the novel was printed in Paris by Shakespeare and Company, the bookshop of Sylvia Beach. The publication faced difficulties, because censorship had banned the book in other countries. The work was eventually circulated abroad. The language and structure of the book posed a challenge for readers and translators. // Ulysses is today regarded as one of the most important works of modernism, and 16 June, the day on which the story takes place, is celebrated as Bloomsday. Its influence on twentieth-century literature is enormous. The book is still studied and discussed throughout the world. Its influence on literature continues to this day, with new studies and translations. Understanding the context of the period helps in interpreting the decisions taken then.

analysis|02-02|1943|Παραδίδεται η γερμανική 6η Στρατιά στο Στάλινγκραντ|The German 6th Army surrenders at Stalingrad|The battle of Stalingrad was among the harshest of the Second World War, with the German army advancing into the city in the summer of 1942. The Soviet forces resisted in street fighting and in every building. Stalin demanded that the city must not give way. Friedrich Paulus commanded the 6th Army. Paulus surrendered together with his generals, in a period of great hunger in the battle. // In November 1942 the Soviet counter-offensive encircled the German army, which was trapped in the city with limited supplies. Hitler forbade retreat. On 2 February 1943 the last German forces in the southern zone of the city surrendered to the Soviets. Hitler declared mourning, and Paulus was later blamed for the surrender. // The defeat was a turning point on the Eastern Front, because German initiative never returned. The losses were enormous, with hundreds of thousands dead and captured. The battle of Stalingrad is today regarded as the most decisive event on the Soviet side of the war. This surrender changed the international image of the German army. The debate over the consequences of the event continues in academic research and in public life. This historical development is still studied by researchers and historians around the world.

analysis|02-02|1943|Τελειώνει η μάχη του Στάλινγκραντ|The battle of Stalingrad ends|The battle of Stalingrad lasted about five months and was one of the bloodiest clashes in history. The city, an important industrial and symbolic hub, had been almost completely destroyed. Soldiers and civilians faced hunger, cold and merciless fighting. Soviet resistance was decisive. The city was gradually rebuilt after the war, with extensive memorials to the battle. // On 2 February 1943 the last German units surrendered, and the fighting in the city came to an end. Thousands of prisoners were taken to camps in the Soviet Union, and many did not return. The victory strengthened the morale of the Soviets and of the Allies. The resistance of the residents and the soldiers became linked with the Soviet national memory. // The battle is regarded as a turning point of the Second World War, because Germany lost the initiative in the east. The history of Stalingrad, which was later renamed Volgograd, remains central to the memory of the war. The city's resistance became a symbol of the endurance of peoples against occupation. Today the city has a memorial dedicated to the battle. This historical development is still studied by researchers and historians around the world. Sources of the period, such as documents and testimonies, are essential material for understanding the events.

analysis|02-02|1990|Ο ντε Κλερκ νομιμοποιεί το ΑΝΚ|De Klerk legalises the ANC|For decades South Africa lived under apartheid, a system of racial segregation that determined education, housing, work and the political rights of the Black majority. The African National Congress resisted this regime with protests, strikes and armed action, and for that reason the government had banned it. Many of its leaders were in prison or in exile, while international pressure for sanctions grew year after year. // On 2 February 1990 President Frederik de Klerk announced to parliament that the ANC would no longer be banned, together with other measures lifting restrictions on political activity and on the press. The government thus recognised that no lasting solution could ignore the party that represented the large majority of Black citizens. The announcement was widely accepted as an important turn, although the path to change was not smooth. // The decision opened the way to the release of Nelson Mandela a few days later and, after long negotiations, to the first multiracial elections in 1994. It showed that apartheid could no longer be maintained by repression. The transition to democracy was accompanied by violence, fear and intense conflict, but it was a decisive step for the country and for the whole continent, as it changed the balance of power in the region.

analysis|02-03|1488|Ο Βαρθολομαίος Ντιάς φτάνει στον κόλπο Μόσελ|Bartolomeu Dias reaches Mossel Bay|At the end of the 15th century Europe was looking for a sea route to the East, in order to have direct access to the trade in spices and textiles without passing through areas controlled by the Ottoman Empire.
